passages.t: ‘Make room for us in your hearts’
passages.happening:
Paul ends the warning he began in 6:14. “Therefore, beloved, since we have these promises, let us cleanse ourselves from everything that defiles body and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God” (verse 1).

Then he comes back to his plea of 6:13. “Make room for us in your hearts. We have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have exploited no one” (verse 2).

He is not trying to shame them. “I do not say this to condemn you. I have said before that you so occupy our hearts that we live and die together with you” (verse 3).

And his words overflow. “Great is my confidence in you; great is my pride in you; I am filled with encouragement; in all our troubles my joy overflows” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
Verse 1 says ‘let us’, not ‘you must’. Paul includes himself. The promises he has just quoted, that God will live among them and be their Father, are the reason for holiness, not a reward for it. ‘Body and spirit’ means the whole person, outward life and inner life alike. ‘Perfecting holiness’ means carrying it through to completion. It is something that grows.

Then Paul turns back to the relationship. ‘Make room for us’ is, word for word, ‘make space for us’. It answers 6:12, where he said their hearts were cramped.

The three denials in verse 2 seem to answer charges. Someone may have said that Paul had wronged them, led people astray, or taken advantage of them, perhaps over money, since the collection was under way. Paul's rivals did take money (11:20). Paul says plainly that he did none of these things.

But he quickly adds that he is not accusing them. ‘We live and die together with you.’ These are words of the closest friendship, of people who share every fortune. Paul is not their employer or their judge. He is bound to them for life.
passages.ot:
‘Perfecting holiness in the fear of God’ echoes God's word to Israel: “For I am the LORD your God; consecrate yourselves, therefore, and be holy, because I am holy” (Leviticus 11:44). Holiness in the Old Testament meant belonging to God and being set apart for him, in the whole of life.

‘The fear of God’ in the Bible is not terror. It is reverence that takes God seriously. “As a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion on those who fear Him” (Psalm 103:13).

A psalm prays for the cleansing Paul speaks of: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me” (Psalm 51:10).
passages.asks: Paul says, ‘let us cleanse ourselves’, putting himself first. Ask what in your own life defiles ‘body and spirit’, and what holiness would look like there. Then ask who has made room for you in their heart, and whether you have made room for them in yours.

passages.happening:
Now the story that stopped at 2:13 begins again. Paul had left Troas for Macedonia, looking for Titus. It was not easy there either. “For when we arrived in Macedonia, our bodies had no rest, but we were pressed from every direction” (verse 5). Paul names it: “conflicts on the outside, fears within” (verse 5).

“But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the arrival of Titus” (verse 6).

And not only by his arrival. Titus had been comforted by the Corinthians, and he brought that comfort with him. “He told us about your longing, your mourning, and your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced all the more” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Look how the story is built. At 2:13 Paul had no peace and went on to Macedonia. Then he turned aside for more than four chapters. Here, at 7:5, he picks up the story at exactly that point, with Macedonia again. Some readers think that shows separate letters were joined. Others think Paul simply turned aside, as people do in heartfelt letters, and came back. These notes do not choose, as the book page says.

‘Conflicts on the outside, fears within.’ Paul does not say what the conflicts were. The churches of Macedonia had faced opposition from the start. And the fears were about Corinth: had his tearful letter broken the friendship for good?

Then God comforted him, and how? By a friend walking through the door. Paul does not say God took away his troubles by a miracle. He says God sent a person. That is often how the comfort of chapter 1 comes.

Titus was a Gentile, a Greek, one of Paul's closest helpers (Galatians 2:3). He had gone to Corinth after Paul's hard letter, to see how it had been received. Ancient letters were carried by people, and the carrier often explained the letter and brought back a report. Titus's report was better than Paul had dared to hope. The church missed Paul, grieved over what had happened, and was eager to stand with him.
passages.ot:
‘God, who comforts the downcast’ is how Isaiah speaks of God, who lives “with the oppressed and humble in spirit, to restore the spirit of the lowly and revive the heart of the contrite” (Isaiah 57:15). The psalm says, “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit” (Psalm 34:18).

The Psalms are honest about fear within. One singer asks himself, “Why are you downcast, O my soul? Why the unease within me? Put your hope in God” (Psalm 42:5).

And the joy of good news after long waiting is in Proverbs: “Like cold water to a weary soul is good news from a distant land” (Proverbs 25:25).
passages.asks: God comforted Paul through Titus. Ask whom God has used to comfort you, often without their knowing it. Then ask whether you could be a Titus to someone this week: a visit, a message, a report of good news, or simply being there. And if you are among the downcast now, notice that Paul was too.

passages.happening:
Paul turns to the letter he had sent. “Even if I caused you sorrow by my letter, I do not regret it. Although I did regret it, I now see that my letter caused you sorrow, but only for a short time” (verse 8).

He is glad, but not that they were hurt. “And now I rejoice, not because you were made sorrowful, but because your sorrow led you to repentance” (verse 9).

Then he names two kinds of sorrow. “Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret, but worldly sorrow brings death” (verse 10).

He shows what their godly sorrow produced: “what earnestness, what eagerness to clear yourselves, what indignation, what alarm, what longing, what zeal, what vindication!” (verse 11).

And he says what his letter was really for. It was not mainly about “the one who did wrong or the one who was harmed” (verse 12). It was so that their own devotion would be made clear to them, before God.
passages.hearers:
Paul admits that he regretted sending the letter for a while. He did not know how it would land. Like any pastor or parent who has spoken a hard word, he worried that he had gone too far. Then the news came, and he saw that the hurt had led somewhere good.

‘Repentance’ is the Greek metanoia. It means a change of mind, but in the Bible it is a turning of the whole person, away from wrong and back toward God.

So what is the difference between the two sorrows? Paul does not define them in detail, but the passage shows the shape. Godly sorrow is sorrow ‘as God intended’. It turns toward God. It leads to a change of heart and life, and it ends in salvation and freedom. No one looks back on it with regret. Worldly sorrow is sorrow that does not turn to God. It may be grief at being caught, or shame about what others think, or bitterness that things went badly. It does not lead to change or to life. It goes round in circles, and in the end it ‘brings death’.

Look at the list in verse 11. It reads like the church coming to life again: in earnest, eager to put things right, angry at the wrong, alarmed, longing for Paul, zealous, wanting justice done. That is what sorrow that turns to God looks like.

‘The one who did wrong’ and ‘the one who was harmed’ point back to the trouble of the painful visit (2:5-11). The one harmed may have been Paul himself, or another member of the church. Paul does not say.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament is full of godly sorrow. When the prophet Nathan confronted King David, David said, “I have sinned against the LORD.” Nathan answered, “The LORD has taken away your sin” (2 Samuel 12:13). David's prayer after that sin is Psalm 51: “Restore to me the joy of Your salvation, and sustain me with a willing spirit” (Psalm 51:12).

The prophets called for it. “So rend your hearts and not your garments, and return to the LORD your God. For He is gracious and compassionate” (Joel 2:13). Ripped clothes were a sign of grief. God asks for a turned heart.

And God receives such sorrow. “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise” (Psalm 51:17).

In the Gospels, Peter denied Jesus three times, “And he went outside and wept bitterly” (Luke 22:62). His sorrow led him back, and the risen Jesus restored him: “Feed My sheep” (John 21:17).

Hebrews 12:17 speaks of Esau, who could find no way to undo what he had done, though he wept. The site's note on Genesis 27:30-40 sets beside it Paul's words here, and says what Hebrews does not mean.
passages.hard:
How can I tell which sorrow I have? What if my guilt will not lift?

Some readers come to this verse already crushed. They have confessed and turned, and yet the guilt stays, heavy and constant. They wonder whether their sorrow is the ‘worldly’ kind, and whether that means they are lost. If that is you, please hear this. A heart that grieves over sin and longs to be right with God is not the mark of someone God has turned away. Worldly sorrow does not care about God. You do.

Godly sorrow leads to salvation ‘without regret’. That means it is meant to end in freedom, not to go on forever. God's answer to sin that is confessed is forgiveness. “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). Jesus said, “the one who comes to Me I will never drive away” (John 6:37). Guilt that keeps coming back after you have confessed is not proof that God has not forgiven you. As the site's note on Genesis 27 says of Hebrews 12, if you are afraid you have gone too far for God to take you back, that door has not been shut.

Sometimes guilt that will not lift needs more than a Bible verse. It can be part of anxiety, depression or a habit of the mind that keeps returning to the same fear. That is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

And a word for anyone who has caused another person sorrow and is tempted to use this passage. Paul did not rejoice that people were hurt. He regretted it, and he wrote in tears. This passage gives no one leave to wound others and call it ‘godly sorrow’.
passages.asks: Paul says godly sorrow leads to a change of life. Think of a time you were sorry. Ask whether it was sorrow over what you had done, or over being found out. What followed? Then ask whether there is something you need to bring to God now, trusting that he receives a broken and contrite heart.

passages.happening:
Paul is encouraged, and he is even more glad because Titus is glad. “For his spirit has been refreshed by all of you” (verse 13).

Paul had spoken well of the Corinthians to Titus before he went. Now he is not embarrassed. “But just as everything we said to you was true, so our boasting to Titus has proved to be true as well” (verse 14).

Titus loves them all the more when he remembers how they received him, “as you welcomed him with fear and trembling” (verse 15).

And Paul ends this part of the letter in joy. “I rejoice that I can have complete confidence in you” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Paul had boasted about the Corinthians to Titus. That was a risk. Titus went to a church that had treated Paul badly. If they had refused him, Paul's words would have been shown false, and he would have been shamed. Instead, the church received Titus well, and Paul's confidence in them proved true.

Notice that the boasting here is boasting about others. Later in this letter Paul will refuse to boast about himself except in his weakness. But he is glad to boast about the people he loves.

‘With fear and trembling’ was a common way of speaking in the Bible for humble respect, not terror. Paul uses it of how believers work out their salvation (Philippians 2:12). The Corinthians received Titus as Paul's messenger, seriously and humbly.

This closes the first great part of the letter. It began with the God of all comfort in trouble (1:3-7). It ends with comfort received, a friendship mended, and confidence restored. That joy gives Paul the ground to ask, in the next two chapters, for the church's help with the gift for Jerusalem.
passages.ot:
‘Fear and trembling’ has Old Testament roots. A psalm says, “Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling” (Psalm 2:11). God esteems the one “who is humble and contrite in spirit, who trembles at My word” (Isaiah 66:2). In the Bible, trembling before God and joy in God go together.

The refreshing of a weary spirit is in Proverbs too: “Like cold water to a weary soul is good news from a distant land” (Proverbs 25:25).

And Paul's joy at a quarrel healed echoes the psalm of a united people: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in harmony!” (Psalm 133:1).
passages.asks: Paul boasted to Titus about the Corinthians, and was glad when it proved true. Ask whom you speak well of when they are not in the room. Ask whether there is a relationship in your life that has been mended, and whether you have thanked God for it. And ask whose spirit you could refresh, as the Corinthians refreshed Titus.
